hops.title: The pale-coat wiring of Siamese cats and white tigers
hops.text: Siamese cats are often cross-eyed, and white tigers sometimes are. In Siamese cats, the reduced pigment that pales the coat comes with unusual visual wiring: some fibers from the temple side of each retina cross to the wrong side of the brain and reach LGN layers meant for the other eye. In 1971 Hubel and Wiesel found no cells driven by both eyes in the cortex serving the cats' peripheral vision. One Siamese raised with both eyes closed did have them, suggesting the squint caused the loss. In 1973 Ray Guillery and Jon Kaas found a similar albinism-type abnormality in one white tiger's brain.

sources.citation: Hubel DH & Wiesel TN, J. Physiol. 218(1):33-62 (1971), PMID 5130620
Guillery RW & Kaas JH, Science 180(4092):1287-1289 (1973), PMID 4707916

image.caption: Siamese cats have unusual pale-coat visual wiring; one white tiger with aligned eyes showed a similar abnormality.

hops.title: After a patch, an adult's covered eye briefly wins
hops.text: Six days with one eye closed, at the peak of a kitten's window, leaves few cortical cells that eye can still drive. So it is tempting to assume an adult's patched eye loses ground too, only more slowly. In 2013, Claudia Lunghi, David Burr and Maria Concetta Morrone patched one eye of healthy adults for 150 minutes, then showed each eye a different striped pattern. With grayscale stripes, the patched eye's pattern stayed visible longer on average during the first 15 minutes. With brightness-matched color stripes, that effect still held 180 minutes later. The authors read it as homeostatic compensation: the adult system briefly turned up the deprived eye.

sources.citation: Lunghi C, Burr DC & Morrone MC, J. Vis. 13(6):1 (2013), PMID 23637272

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student removing a translucent eye patch beside shutter goggles and a screen showing two differently tilted striped patterns.
image.caption: After 150 minutes under a patch, an adult's covered eye briefly wins more of the contest between the eyes.

hops.title: The neurobiologist who gained stereo vision as an adult
hops.text: For years, Mount Holyoke College neurobiologist Susan Barry taught students that the brain is highly malleable in infancy but loses the capacity to rewire in adulthood. Cross-eyed since early infancy, she learned to shut down one eye's input to avoid double vision, and she grew up without stereo vision, the depth the brain computes by comparing the two eyes' images. In 2002 she began optometric vision therapy to train both eyes to aim at the same point. Buildings on street corners started to loom toward her like the bows of giant ships, and tree branches reached out into space. She began teaching adult plasticity differently.

sources.citation: Susan Barry faculty profile, Mount Holyoke College

image.caption: After growing up without stereo vision, Susan Barry gained it as an adult through vision therapy.
